concept.name: Volatility targeting
concept.definition: A portfolio management rule that scales exposure inversely to an estimate of current volatility so that portfolio risk stays near a constant target level: taking less risk when volatility is high and more when it is low.
concept.intuition: If the market is twice as wild, hold half as much: keeping risk (not capital) constant smooths the return stream and prevents risk from ballooning exactly in crises.
concept.mechanics: Estimate volatility (trailing realized or exponentially weighted), set the exposure weight w = sigma_target / sigma_estimate, rebalance periodically, and cap the weight by a leverage ceiling. Moreira and Muir document that such volatility-managed portfolios historically raised factor Sharpe ratios because volatility changes were not fully offset by proportional changes in expected returns.
concept.formula: w_t = min( sigma_target / sigma_hat_t, w_max ), where sigma_target is the desired annualized volatility and sigma_hat_t the current volatility estimate; exposure exceeds 1 (leverage) when sigma_hat_t < sigma_target.
concept.failure_modes: Volatility estimates lag regime shifts, leaving exposure highest right before a vol spike when the estimation window is slow, and gaps can move prices faster than rebalancing de-risks. Leverage caps and transaction costs constrain implementation, and the documented Sharpe improvement is an empirical finding, not a law.
concept.misconceptions: Volatility targeting is not return forecasting: it times risk, not direction. A constant-volatility portfolio is not a low-risk portfolio when the target itself is set aggressively.
concept.example: With a 10% volatility target, an asset estimated at 20% volatility is held at 0.5 weight; if estimated volatility later falls to 8%, the weight rises to 1.25, subject to the leverage cap.

citations.source: Moreira, A. and Muir, T.: Volatility-Managed Portfolios (SSRN)
Moreira and Muir - Volatility Managed Portfolios (NBER Working Paper 22208)
